'''Julia Mae Phillips''' (born August 17, 1954)<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Phillips, Julia M.|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11508005.html|access-date=2021-05-18|website=history.aip.org}}</ref> is an American physicist. She began her career in [[materials research]] on thin films on [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]] and has transitioned into leadership roles in [[science policy]]. She currently serves on the [[National Science Board]].

== Early life and education ==
Phillips was born in 1954 in [[Freeport, Illinois|Freeport]], [[Illinois]].<ref name=":4" /> Her father and grandfathers were doctors. Growing up in a rural area, she often went out stargazing.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|last=Madsen|first=Lynnette|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JPSlCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA450|title=Successful Women Ceramic and Glass Scientists and Engineers: 100 Inspirational Profiles|date=2016-02-01|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-118-73360-8|language=en}}</ref> When she was in fifth grade, a teacher showed her how to triangulate to calculate distances, which further motivated her to study astronomy. Her mother was supportive and bought Phillips and her brother science kits. Phillips found the quantitative and objective nature of science appealing.<ref name=":5" /> She graduated from [[Freeport High School (Illinois)|Freeport High School]] in 1972 as valedictorian.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|last=Robinson-Avila|first=Kevin|date=2007-11-11|title=The matchmaker|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/albuquerque/stories/2007/11/12/story14.html|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.bizjournals.com}}</ref>

She completed an undergraduate degree in physics at the [[College of William & Mary]] in 1976.<ref name=":6" /> Her undergraduate honors thesis was entitled ''Neutral differential cross section measurements in collisions of cl ̄with the rare gases''.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Neutral differential cross section measurements in collisions of cl ̄with the rare gases|date=1976|language=English|first=Julia Mae|last=Phillips|oclc=9010309}}</ref> She was mentored by John Delos.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-06-23|title=Julia Phillips|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/44401|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.aip.org|language=en}}</ref>

Phillips went on to complete a master's and PhD at [[Yale University]].<ref name=":1" /> Shortly before completing her PhD, Phillips's supervisor had a nervous breakdown, which was a lesson to Phillips in reaching out for assistance when needed.<ref name=":5" /> Her 1981 doctoral thesis was on the topic of ''Electronic excitation of helium and krypton by electron impact''.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Electronic excitation of helium and krypton by electron impact.|date=1981|place=New Haven] CT|language=English|first=Julia Mae|last=Phillips|oclc=702698339}}</ref>

== Career ==
Phillips worked at [[Bell Labs]] starting in 1981.<ref name=":1" /> She has noted that the environment at Bell Labs was excellent for research freedom and collaboration and could be a model for new research centers.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Harvard's incomparable Venky|url=https://www.seas.harvard.edu/news/2014/09/harvards-incomparable-venky|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.seas.harvard.edu}}</ref> She was a member of the technical staff until 1988 when was promoted to a supervisor role.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Julia Mae Phillips, Ph.D., Presented with the Albert Nelson Marquis Lifetime Achievement Award by Marquis Who's Who|url=https://www.24-7pressrelease.com/press-release/459919/julia-mae-phillips-phd-presented-with-the-albert-nelson-marquis-lifetime-achievement-award-by-marquis-whos-who|access-date=2021-05-18|website=24-7 Press Release Newswire|language=en}}</ref>

Phillips researched thin film epitaxial materials and oxides on semiconductors for potential electronics applications.<ref name=":1" /> She dubbed this work "lunatic fringe molecular beam epitaxy".<ref name=":5" /> She also contributed to high-temperature superconductors and transparent conducting materials.<ref name=":5" />

In 1995, she joined [[Sandia National Laboratories]] and in 2001, she became a Director of the Sandia Physical, Chemical, and Nano Sciences Center. Between 2005 and 2007, she was also a Director of the Center for Integrated Nanotechnologies (CINT).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=2008 George E. Pake Prize Recipient|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Phillips&first_nm=Julia&year=2008|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref> Phillips's last role at Sandia was as Vice President and Chief Technology Officer. She retired in 2015, though remains an Emeritus Director.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=stephanie.shaw@nist.gov|date=2019-04-29|title=Julia Phillips - Biography|url=https://www.nist.gov/director/vcat/julia-phillips-biography|access-date=2021-05-18|website=NIST|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> In [[New Mexico]], Phillips was a major figure in the nanotechnology industry and advised the governor's office on how to foster tech start-ups and interest students in science careers. She has been praised for her energy and commitment to high-quality research with a positive, long-term impact. She managed 180 people and a budget over $45 million.<ref name=":6" />

In 2016, Phillips was appointed to the [[National Science Board]] by President [[Barack Obama]] on a six year term. This role involves advising the [[National Science Foundation]] and the president on matters related to science policy and innovation in the [[United States]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-10-31|title=President Obama Appoints Morgan Research Division VP To National Science Board|url=https://news.morgan.edu/president-obama-appoints-morgan-research-division-vp-to-national-science-board/|access-date=2021-05-18|website=Morgan State University Newsroom|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Labs|first=Sandia|date=2016-10-27|title=Sandia National Laboratories: Former Sandia VP named to National Science Board|url=https://www.sandia.gov/news/publications/labnews/articles/2016/28-10/phillips_NSB.html|access-date=2021-05-18|website=Sandia Labs|language=en}}</ref> Phillips was excited to take on the responsibility and ensure that scientific research in the US remains of a high caliber.<ref name=":2" />

In 2020, Phillips became a President’s Distinguished Scholar at the [[University of Vermont]], a mentorship role to support leadership and technology transfer.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|title=Renowned Scientist Becomes First President's Distinguished Scholar at UVM|url=https://www.uvm.edu/uvmnews/news/renowned-scientist-becomes-first-presidents-distinguished-scholar-uvm|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.uvm.edu|language=en}}</ref> She is a proponent of interdisciplinary materials research to solve problems related to energy, sustainability and medicine. She believes that a variety of perspectives and domains of expertise will lead to new breakthroughs. Phillips serves on the External Advisory Board of [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]'s Materials Research Laboratory.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Interdisciplinary materials science a key to progress|url=https://news.mit.edu/2017/mit-materials-day-symposium-1106|access-date=2021-05-18|website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology|date=5 November 2017 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Introducing the Materials Research Laboratory at MIT|url=https://news.mit.edu/2017/introducing-mit-materials-research-laboratory-mrl-1010|access-date=2021-05-18|website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology|date=10 October 2017 |language=en}}</ref>

Phillips has chaired the [[American Physical Society]] (APS) Division of Condensed Matter Physics and served as president of the [[Materials Research Society]] in 1995.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Past MRS Presidents|url=https://www.mrs.org/about-mrs/the-society/past-mrs-presidents|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.mrs.org}}</ref> She has been an editor for numerous physics journals including [[Applied Physics Letters]], [[Journal of Applied Physics]], [[Applied Physics Reviews]], and [[Journal of Materials Research and Technology|Journal of Materials Research]]. She holds five patents.<ref name=":0" /> From 2016 to 2020, she was Home Secretary of the [[National Academy of Engineering]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Julia M. Phillips|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/julia-m-phillips|access-date=2021-05-18|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|language=en}}</ref> She is a founding member of Expert Connect.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Expert Connect|url=https://nationalmedals.org/expert-connect/|access-date=2021-05-18|website=National Science and Technology Medals Foundation|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Awards and honours ==

* 2019 5 Sigma Physicist Award from the [[American Physical Society]] for her work as an advocate for reducing nuclear risk.<ref>{{Cite web|title=5 Sigma Physicist Award|url=http://www.aps.org/policy/5-sigma.cfm|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Ayala|first=Christine|date=2018-08-04|title=Walking the nuclear risk tightrope|url=https://thehill.com/opinion/energy-environment/400366-walking-the-nuclear-risk-tightrope|access-date=2021-05-18|website=TheHill|language=en}}</ref>
*2018 Inductee, [[Albert Nelson Marquis]] Lifetime Achievement.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Administrator|first=Who's Who Site|date=2018-12-27|title=Julia Mae Phillips|url=https://wwlifetimeachievement.com/2018/12/27/julia-mae-phillips/|access-date=2021-05-18|website=Who's Who Lifetime Achievement|language=en-US}}</ref>
*2016 Appointment to the [[National Science Board]].<ref name=":2" />
*2010 Fellow of the [[Materials Research Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=List of MRS Fellows {{!}} Materials science awards|url=https://www.mrs.org/careers-advancement/awards/spring-awards/mrs-fellows/list-of-mrs-fellows|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.mrs.org}}</ref>
*2008 [[George E. Pake Prize]] ''for her leadership and pioneering research in materials physics for industrial and national security applications''.<ref name=":0" />
* 2005 Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name=":3" />
*2004 Member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] ''for leadership and distinguished research in the epitaxy of dissimilar materials''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Dr. Julia M. Phillips|url=https://nae.edu/30251/Dr-Julia-M-Phillips|access-date=2021-05-18|website=NAE Website}}</ref>
*2004 [[Wilbur Cross Medal]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2004-05-24|title=Yale Awards Wilbur Cross Medals to Graduate School Alumni|url=https://news.yale.edu/2004/05/24/yale-awards-wilbur-cross-medals-graduate-school-alumni|access-date=2021-05-18|website=YaleNews|language=en}}</ref>
* 2002 Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Elected Fellows {{!}} American Association for the Advancement of Science|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/listing|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.aaas.org|language=en}}</ref> 
*2002 Horizon Award from the [[United States Department of Labor|US Department of Labor]] Women's Bureau.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Daily News Briefs|url=https://www.photonics.com/Articles/Daily_News_Briefs/a14114|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.photonics.com}}</ref> 
*1996 Materials Research Society Woody Award.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Woody Award Recipients {{!}} MRS Awards|url=https://www.mrs.org/careers-advancement/awards/fall-awards/mrs-woody-white-service-award/woody-award-recipients|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.mrs.org}}</ref> 
*1993 Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] ''for her contributions to the understanding of the growth mechanisms and properties of epitaxial heterostructures involving structurally and electrically dissimilar materials''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm|access-date=2021-05-18|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
In 1989, Phillips married a now-retired neurophysiologist, John A. Connor. Phillips and her husband are both musicians. She plays the flute and he plays the piano. The couple had two daughters. One daughter, Julia Connor, is a violinist<ref name=":6" /> while the other, Bridget Connor, is a chemist.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Julia Phillips|url=https://www.engineergirl.org/2945/Julia-Phillips|access-date=2021-05-18|website=EngineerGirl}}</ref>
